summary: Describes an architecture for DDoS Open Threat Signaling within and between domains. It does not specify protocols and instead defines the relationships, components and concepts of a DOTS deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: DOTS gives networks a shared way to ask for help during a DDoS attack. This RFC explains the roles and communication paths, while separate documents specify the protocols.

subtitle: The components and relationships used to coordinate DDoS mitigation requests.

tldr.problem: A network under a distributed denial-of-service attack may need another domain to help filter traffic. The parties need agreed roles and a way to exchange requests and status.
tldr.mechanism: DOTS defines clients, servers, gateways, and signal and data channels. A client asks a server for mitigation; the server may pass the request to a mitigator and report its status.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines architecture, not wire protocols. It describes session setup, signaling arrangements, request triggers, and security requirements.

today: RFC 8811 is an Informational IETF document published in August 2020. It describes the architecture used by the DOTS signal channel protocol in RFC 8782 and data channel protocol in RFC 8783.

sections.title: The DOTS Components and Channels
sections.content:
A DOTS deployment can include an attack target, a DOTS client near the target, a DOTS server in a service domain, and a mitigator that filters traffic. DOTS covers the client-server interface; it does not specify how a target detects an attack or how a mitigator filters it.

The signal channel carries mitigation requests, status, and heartbeats and is designed to keep contact during severe congestion. The optional data channel carries configuration such as resource aliases, drop-lists, accept-lists, and filters. The data channel needs reliable delivery, but the architecture does not promise that it will work during an attack.
sections.plainLanguage: A client asks a server for mitigation, and the server may ask a mitigator to filter traffic. The signal channel carries urgent requests and status; the optional data channel carries configuration.

sections.title: Clients, Servers and Gateways
sections.content:
A client starts mitigation requests and can report target health or mitigation results. A server authenticates and authorizes clients, tracks requests, and reports the actual mitigation scope and status. A request is advisory: a server may refuse it or lack the capacity to act.

A DOTS gateway combines a server role facing downstream agents with a client role facing upstream agents. It must terminate and start new sessions on each side. A client can use several servers, but uncoordinated mitigation requests can divert the same traffic in conflicting ways.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks for help, and the server decides whether to act and reports what happened. A gateway joins separate DOTS sessions and acts as a server on one side and a client on the other.

sections.title: Sessions and Heartbeats
sections.content:
A DOTS session can use a signal channel, a data channel, or both. The server links the channels using the client's identity. A signal session uses one TCP or UDP connection and TLS or DTLS; a data session uses TCP and TLS.

Before connecting, the parties are assumed to have agreed on service terms and the client has the needed connection and cryptographic information. Both agents send periodic heartbeats. Either may treat the signal session as ended after a prolonged absence of the other side's heartbeat.
sections.plainLanguage: The client and server establish an authenticated connection before they need it. They exchange regular heartbeats so each side can tell whether the other is still reachable.

sections.title: Signaling Modes and Request Triggers
sections.content:
DOTS can use direct signaling, redirect a client to another server, or let one domain ask another for additional mitigation through recursive signaling. A service address using anycast can reach different servers as routing changes, but a new server may lack the session's security state. Network address translation also means a client may need to identify the public addresses that correspond to protected internal systems.

The architecture does not prescribe when to request mitigation. An operator may issue a request manually, define conditions such as traffic rates or resource exhaustion, or request mitigation when heartbeats stop. Loss of signal can have causes other than an attack, so that trigger may cause unnecessary cost or affect network performance.
sections.plainLanguage: A request can go directly to a server, be redirected, or be passed through another domain. Operators choose when to request mitigation, but lost heartbeats do not always mean an attack.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies impersonation, message injection, and signal blocking as major threats. Fake messages could start or stop traffic redirection or alter filtering lists. DOTS agents must authenticate each other, and a server must check that the client may request mitigation for the named resources.

Topology, telemetry, and mitigation details may be sensitive and should be protected at rest according to local policy. Operators should monitor clients because a compromised client could repeatedly request and withdraw mitigation. DOTS servers need adequate network and host protection.
sections.plainLanguage: Each agent must prove its identity, and a server must check that a client controls the resources it names. Operators should also protect stored network details and monitor clients for misuse.
